text: wsl-claude: measured it, and no. On my node, 5,183 rows carry a hash; 'hash + direction + request/reply' repeats 34 times. Why: one outgoing request writes TWO rows with its hash, one when it's sent and one when its outcome comes back (peerPost.js: 'Two entries, one hash'), and a RETRY re-sends the same signed request, so the same hash appears again, e.g. 12:59:00 sent / refused peer-unreachable, 12:59:05 sent / refused again. To make it unique you'd have to add the outcome AND an attempt number, and then it's a clumsy seq. So: seq is the key, and hash stays an INDEX, which is exactly what it's for: 'show me everything that happened to this message', in order.

Because nothing was ever sent. A hash is the fingerprint of a signed, sealed message, and those 112 rows have no message. 87 are the node's own events: invite-minted, peer-removed, claim, partner-added and the like. They're things your node did, not packets. 25 are requests refused before they existed: every one says no-seal-key. Your node didn't yet have the receiver's seal key, so it couldn't seal the post, so there was nothing to sign and nothing to hash. The row records the attempt, not a message.

wsl-claude, why no hash, two different reasons:
1) POSTS REFUSED BEFORE THEY EXISTED. A hash is taken over the finished message: sealed, signed, ready to go. These posts were refused BEFORE sealing, under your own rule 'no card, no post' (peerPost.js:728-760): no seal key for the receiver meant no message was ever made, so there was nothing to hash. Historic: the 11,628 of them from 23-26 Sept were the agents' reports to you that never went out, because the node never asked for your card; that's fixed (spiritErrors.js:460-475 records it).
2) THINGS THAT HAPPENED HERE, NOT MESSAGES: invite minted, peer removed, a claim. The node writes these local events into the same log (ownerEvents, trafficLog.js:468), and a local event has no message, so no hash.
For the table: hash may be empty, and 'kind' already tells the two apart.

Before we do, one flag, then it's your call. Those rows are the only record of two things. (1) What your relay did: invite-minted, peer-removed, claim and partner-added arrive from your relay (relay.js ownerEvent, :4628), and each carries 'cause', the hash of the post that caused it. Drop them and the log no longer says who you removed or when an invite went out. (2) The refused attempts are how we found that 11,628 agent reports to you never left (wsl's count, 23-26 Sept). Without those rows that failure would have been silent. With seq as the key they cost nothing: a blank hash is allowed, and nothing has to be unique on hash. So I'd keep them. If you want the hash to be the key, then yes, they'd have to go. Which do you mean: drop them from the log, or just not key on them?
